title: Forms that post without a maze of scripts
metaTitle: Forms that land where you can see
excerpt: A form needs a place to land, a confirmation on the page, and a log of failures. A widget you cannot debug on launch day is a risk.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf. The plain shelf fits a piece about a form with a visible place to land.
caption: The message needs a shelf you can check. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should a website form submit to?
faqs.answer: To a route or server action you control, which stores the message or sends it to an inbox you can open. Keeping a row and sending an email is the sturdy version: the email alerts you, and the row remains if the mailbox does not. The sender should see a confirmation on the page either way.

faqs.question: How should form errors be shown?
faqs.answer: In text, on the field that failed, without clearing what the person already typed. A red outline alone is not enough. WCAG expects an input error to be identified and described in text. Server failures belong in a log your team can read, separate from the sender's confirmation that their note was stored.

faqs.question: When is a third-party form widget a problem?
faqs.answer: When it is the only way the company can be contacted and you cannot see why it failed. Blocked scripts, an outage on the vendor's side, and errors you cannot restyle all show up at the worst time. Use your own form for the primary path. It should still post if the enhancement script does not run.

markdown:
A website form backend is the place a message lands, the confirmation the sender sees, and a way for you to notice failures. Those three are the form. The fields are the easy part. A widget you cannot debug at 6pm on launch day is a risk, because launch day is when the form matters and when the person who installed the widget may be busy.

Own the path. A form can post to a server action or a route you control, validate there, and store or forward the message where you can read it. The page stays a page. The submission is a record.

## A place to land

Decide the inbox before you draw the form. An email to a named address, a row in your database, or both. Both is the calmer choice. The email is the alert. The row is the record that survives a filter, a full mailbox, and a teammate who deletes messages to feel organized.

If you store the row, store the fields you asked for, the time, and whether the notification was sent. You do not need a customer-relationship maze for a site contact form. You need to answer the question "did Tuesday's note arrive?" without guessing.

Say, on the form, what will happen. "We read this and reply by email." Only promise a speed you will keep. A false "within the hour" is worse than a plain "we reply by email." If the form is for a job application or a press note, say which address it reaches so people do not use it for a billing question.

Spam will arrive. Handle it without making the honest sender solve a puzzle. A honeypot field hidden from people, a rate limit, and a server-side check will stop the lazy floods. A captcha that fails on a phone, from a third-party script, is the widget problem again. Add the heavy challenge only if the simple checks are losing, and test it on the device your founders actually use.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes the guidelines as a shared standard for web content, including the understandable principle. When a form detects an error, the field in error has to be identified and described in text. That requirement is reason enough to render errors yourself. A widget that only outlines a box in red, inside a frame you cannot restyle, will fail the standard and fail the person who cannot see the color.

## A confirmation that is part of the page

After a successful post, the page should say so in the document, not only in an email the sender may not see for an hour. "Received. We will reply by email." Leave the message on screen. Do not clear the form and hope they noticed a toast.

If the email notification fails and the row was saved, the sender still deserves that confirmation, and you deserve a visible failure on your side. Those are different events. The sender did their part. Your mailer did not. Log the mailer failure next to the row so you can reply by hand. A green checkmark that means "we tried" is a lie. A green checkmark that means "stored" is honest if the sentence says you have it.

Validation errors are a confirmation of a different kind. They confirm you did not send yet, and they say why. Put the text at the field and in a summary at the top if there are several. Keep what they typed. A form that wipes a paragraph because the email was missing will not be filled in a second time.

Disable the button while the request is in flight so you do not store doubles, and if the request takes long enough to notice, say that it is sending. Then resolve to the success sentence or the error. A button that stays on "Sending" with no resolution is the silent failure. Time it out in the interface, keep the text, and tell them to try again.

## A way to see failures

You need a log you can open without the widget vendor. Failed validation can stay on the page, because the sender has to see it. Failed delivery, a down database, a rejected address, an exception you did not expect: those need a record with the time and the reason, visible to the team.

A third-party form tool can be fine for a temporary campaign if you accept the trade. You cannot restyle the errors, you cannot be sure the script loaded, and on launch night you may be reading their status page instead of your own log. For the main way a company asks to be contacted, that trade is expensive. Use the tool for a side experiment if you want. Keep the primary form on your server.

Script blockers and flaky networks are part of the test, not an edge case. The form should work as HTML. A `form` element with an action, a button of type submit, and server handling will post even when your enhancement script does not run. Progressive enhancement is the difference between a form and a picture of a form. If the page is server rendered, the form is already in the document. Do not replace it with a div that only becomes a form after hydration.

Watch the network tab once. You want a single post to your origin, a clear status code, and a body you can explain. A page that calls three vendors on submit, and shows success when the first one returns, will lose notes in the gap. Pick one place to land and treat the others as optional notifications.

## Fields worth asking for

Ask for what you need to reply, and for the context that stops a vague "hello" from taking three emails to unpack. Name, email, and what they want is enough for an intro conversation. Company and the page they were on can be useful. A required phone number, a required budget dropdown with invented ranges, and a required "how did you hear about us" will cost you the notes you wanted.

Label every field. Placeholders disappear. The label stays. Group the fields in the order a person can answer them, and make the primary button say what it does: "Send the note," not "Submit."

If you must route the note, ask with one plain question. "Is this about a project, or about something else?" Two paths are enough. A matrix of departments on a five-person company is theater. Route it in the inbox if you are unsure. A misrouted email you can forward is better than a form the sender abandoned.

File uploads need a limit you tell them, a type you accept, and a virus-shaped caution: store them as files, do not execute them, and do not put them on a public URL. Most company forms do not need an upload on the first contact. Add it when a real workflow requires it, with the same confirmation and the same log.

## Launch day, at 6pm

The risk in the angle is specific. The site is live, a partner just shared the URL, and the form fails. You need to know that it failed, and you need to know why, without a vendor's dashboard login you have not used in four months.

Before you launch, post a note yourselves, from a phone, on the network you will not be on later. Confirm the row, the email, and the sentence on the page. Then break it on purpose in staging: empty required field, bad email, server error. Each break should produce a sentence you can read, and the server error should produce a log line you can find.

Write down where the log is. A log nobody can locate is not a log. If the only signal is an uncaught exception in a platform you rarely open, add a message to the address that already receives the forms: "A submission was stored but the notification failed," or "A submission failed before it was stored." Keep that message short and rare so it is not ignored.

Do not discover the failure from a stranger's screenshot. The confirmation and the log exist so you hear it first.

## After it is quiet

A form that works is boring, and boring is the goal. Review it when you change the site's layout, when you change email providers, and when you add a new required field. A new required field is a product change. It will drop the completion rate of a form that used to be easy, and it will create a new error sentence you have to write.

Keep the success sentence in the same voice as the rest of the site. This is not the place for a joke that makes a nervous sender wonder whether the note was real. Received, and what happens next. Then stop.

The person who writes the page around the form needs to see that page before anyone else does. [Previewing a draft before it is public](/blog/previewing-a-draft-before-it-is-public) is the next piece. The writer should see the real template, including the form, before the URL is a public URL. A preview that looks different from the site creates a second design, and the form is usually where that second design shows up.

If you want a form that posts to a place you can see, with a confirmation you can stand behind, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the fields you think you need. The useful version is usually shorter.
